items.name: Portable water filter
items.need: A small filter lets you make doubtful tap water or collected water safer to drink when you cannot boil it, and it fits in a grab bag.
items.how_to_choose: Look for a hollow-fiber filter from a known brand with a stated pore size of 0.2 micron or smaller and published lab results. These filters remove bacteria and parasites but not viruses, chemicals, fuel or heavy metals, so pair them with bleach or tablets when sewage may be in the water. One that threads onto an ordinary 28 mm drink bottle lets you fill containers at the sink instead of only sipping through it. A 28 mm thread is the narrow soda-bottle size: it does not screw onto a wide-mouth bottle such as a 63 mm Nalgene. If your bottle is wide-mouthed, fill the filter's own pouch or a narrow 28 mm bottle with the doubtful water and squeeze it through the filter into your bottle. Check whether the filter comes with a pouch; not all do. Most hollow-fiber filters are ruined if they freeze after first use, so store them indoors and do not leave one in a cold car or on a winter balcony.

qty.note: One filter for every two adults, and at least one per household.

items.already_own: A backpacking squeeze or pump filter from Sawyer, LifeStraw, Katadyn, Platypus or MSR that you already own is fine if it has never frozen while wet, still flows after backflushing, and is under its rated volume. A fridge pitcher or tap-mounted carbon filter is not a substitute: most are not rated for bacteria or parasites. If you bought a filter cheaply from an unknown marketplace seller, treat it as suspect and replace it.

safety_notes.text: Portable filters do not remove all germs and do not remove viruses. To remove bacteria a filter needs an absolute pore size of 0.3 micron or smaller, and 1 micron or smaller for parasites such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium. The squeeze, straw and gravity filters on this page are 0.1 to 0.2 micron, so they do not stop viruses.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Use two steps when water may carry sewage: filter first, then disinfect with chlorine, chlorine dioxide or iodine to kill the viruses and bacteria a filter leaves behind.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Boiling is the most reliable way to kill germs. Bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute. CDC says 3 minutes above 6,500 feet; EPA says 3 minutes above 5,000 feet (1,000 m). Using 3 minutes above 5,000 feet satisfies both.
safety_notes.source_title: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water

safety_notes.text: Water that contains fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting. Use bottled water or another source.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Floodwater can contain human and animal waste and household, medical and industrial hazardous waste, including chemicals. Do not filter or treat floodwater for drinking; stay out of it and use stored or bottled water.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: Floodwater

items.name: Household gravity water filter
items.need: If you shelter at home for two to four weeks under a boil-water notice or with collected water, a gravity filter treats several gallons a day without fuel or power.
items.how_to_choose: Buy only a system whose germ-removal claims are backed by a certificate or by published lab tests, and check what the test actually covers. A countertop urn stands about 20 inches tall, takes water poured in the top and keeps about 2 gallons of filtered water behind a tap; a bag-style gravity filter hangs from a door hook or shower rod and folds flat in a drawer. Ordinary filters (ceramic candles and 0.2 micron membranes) still need a disinfection step for viruses; a purifier (0.02 micron) does both. None of these makes water with fuel, chemicals or floodwater safe. If money is tight, the budget pick plus bleach does the same job as the pricier ones, in smaller batches.

qty.note: Optional extra: stored water, boiling and bleach already cover a household. If you choose to have one, one system per household.

items.already_own: A backpacking gravity or squeeze filter you already own will do the same job in smaller batches. A countertop urn such as a Berkey is not a substitute unless its filter elements have an independent certificate or published lab tests for bacteria and parasites; see the warnings below. Fridge pitchers and tap-mounted carbon filters improve taste but most are not rated for germs, so do not rely on them during a boil-water notice.

safety_notes.text: Portable filters do not remove viruses. After filtering, add a disinfectant such as chlorine or chlorine dioxide to kill remaining viruses and bacteria, or boil the water.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Boiling is the best way to kill germs: a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes at altitude (above 5,000 feet per EPA, above 6,500 feet per CDC).
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Boiling and disinfection do not destroy heavy metals, salts or most other chemicals. Do not use water with floating material, a dark color or a questionable smell.
safety_notes.source_title: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water

safety_notes.text: Water containing fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting; use bottled water or a different source.
safety_notes.source_title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

safety_notes.text: Floodwater can carry sewage and chemical, biological and radiological hazardous waste. Do not collect, filter and drink it.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: Floodwater

safety_notes.text: Store at least one gallon of water per person per day. Let cloudy water settle or strain it through coffee filters or layers of clean cloth before treating it.

item_flags: Berkey is not recommended: in 2022 and 2023 EPA issued stop-sale orders saying Black Berkey filter elements were sold with germ-killing claims without the required pesticide registration. These are stop-sale orders, not a recall.

items.name: Water treatment tablets
items.need: Tablets weigh almost nothing, keep for years and disinfect water when you cannot boil it, which makes them the backup for a grab bag and for viruses that filters miss.
items.how_to_choose: Buy only tablets with an EPA registration number on the pack, and follow the pack: each brand has its own tablet size, amount of water and wait, and the pack's directions are the ones written for that tablet. Chlorine dioxide tablets are the only kind that also kill Cryptosporidium, and their label wait is 4 hours. Chlorine (NaDCC) tablets are quicker but are not a flat 30 minutes: the label EPA accepted for Aquatabs says to mix well for at least 10 minutes and then let the water stand for 30, and it makes no claim for Cryptosporidium. Tablets do not remove dirt or chemicals, so strain or filter cloudy water first. They are costly for treating all of a household's water for two weeks: use stored water, boiling and bleach for the bulk, and keep tablets for the grab bag and as a backup.

qty.rule: 3 days of treated water for each person (3 gallons each), divided by what one pack treats and rounded up
qty.note: Tablets are the backup, so the count is 3 days of water for each person: 3 gallons. One pack of 30 Micropur tablets treats about 8 gallons (30 liters), which covers two people for 3 days; a household of three or four needs two packs. Treating all your water for 14 days with tablets alone would take two packs per person; this count leaves that out, because stored water, boiling and bleach cover the bulk.

items.already_own: Tablets you already have are usable if the foil is intact and the printed expiry date has not passed. Check the active ingredient: chlorine dioxide and NaDCC are fine; old iodine tablets are a last resort and CDC advises against them for pregnant people and those with thyroid problems, and for more than a few weeks' use.

safety_notes.text: Follow the label on tablets and drops; each product is made for a specific amount of water. They kill viruses and bacteria but may not kill parasites. Iodine and chlorine tablets do not kill Cryptosporidium. Chlorine dioxide tablets do if used correctly.

safety_notes.text: Avoid iodine-treated water if you are pregnant, have thyroid problems or are sensitive to iodine, and nobody should drink it for more than a few weeks.

safety_notes.text: Disinfection tablets vary in strength; follow the instructions on the label. If water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter first.

items.name: Plain unscented bleach and a dropper
items.need: A small bottle of plain bleach is the cheapest way to disinfect many gallons of clear water when you cannot boil it.
items.how_to_choose: Read the label, not the front of the bottle. You want regular unscented liquid bleach that says 'disinfecting' or 'kills germs', shows an EPA Reg. No., and states its sodium hypochlorite strength (5% to 9%). Look for drinking-water directions on the label too: if the bottle has them, they are the ones to follow. Buy the smallest bottle you can find, write the purchase date on it, and replace it every year because bleach weakens with age. Keep a clean medicine dropper taped to the bottle, since doses are counted in drops.

qty.note: One small bottle and one dropper per household. Even an 11 oz bottle treats hundreds of gallons.

items.already_own: Bleach already under the sink is fine if the label says it disinfects, it is unscented and not 'splashless', it states 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite, and it is less than a year old and kept at room temperature. If the label gives its own drinking-water dose, use it. The label on Clorox's 7.5% bleach (EPA registration 5813-120) gives 4 drops per quart, or 25 drops (about a quarter teaspoon) for 1.75 gallons, a 30-minute wait, and a second dose with 15 more minutes if the water has no slight chlorine smell. Keep the label with the kit. Any clean medicine dropper or oral syringe works for measuring.

safety_notes.text: The bottle's own label comes first. CDC says to follow the instructions on the bleach label for disinfecting drinking water. Only if the label gives none, check that it is plain unscented bleach of 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite and use CDC's table: 2 drops per quart or liter, or 8 drops per gallon of clear water. Double it if the water is cloudy, colored or very cold. Stir and wait at least 30 minutes before drinking.

safety_notes.text: The label EPA accepted for Clorox's 7.5% bleach (registration 5813-120, July 8, 2024) has its own directions for emergency drinking water: strain or settle the water, add 4 drops per quart, or 25 drops (a quarter teaspoon) for 1.75 gallons, and let it stand 30 minutes. It should then smell slightly of chlorine; if not, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes. The label says the product works against viruses and bacteria only, and that it will not make chemically contaminated water drinkable.

safety_notes.text: Use only regular, unscented chlorine bleach labeled for disinfection. Do not use scented or color-safe bleach or bleach with added cleaners. Use fresh bleach, or bleach stored at room temperature for less than one year. Measure with a clean dropper.

safety_notes.text: Boiling is preferred when you can do it: rolling boil for 1 minute, 3 minutes at altitude (above 5,000 feet per EPA, above 6,500 feet per CDC).

safety_notes.text: Chlorine does not kill Cryptosporidium, and bleach does nothing for chemicals: boiling and disinfection do not destroy heavy metals, salts or most other chemicals, and water with fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe at home. Filter first, then disinfect, when parasites are a concern.

items.name: Pre-filter and chlorine check supplies
items.need: Straining cloudy water first makes boiling, bleach and tablets work properly and keeps filters from clogging; a chlorine strip is an optional check that bleach-treated water has chlorine in it.
items.how_to_choose: For pre-filtering, any clean paper coffee filter, paper towel or tightly woven clean cloth does the job; no special product is needed. For checking, buy strips that read free chlorine specifically, in small steps between 0 and about 4 mg/L; pool strips and total-chlorine strips are too coarse. No home test tells you water is free of germs or chemicals. A strip shows only that some chlorine is present: it is never proof of safety, and it does not tell you when the water is ready.

qty.note: One pack of coffee filters for every household. The chlorine strips in the Cadillac tier are optional.

items.already_own: Coffee filters, paper towels or a clean cotton cloth already in the kitchen are enough for straining. Pool or aquarium test strips are a rough stand-in only if they read free chlorine, are in date and have been kept dry.

safety_notes.text: If water is cloudy, filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter, or let it settle and pour off the clear water, before boiling or disinfecting. Straining does not remove germs by itself.

safety_notes.text: A chlorine strip shows only that some chlorine is present. It does not decide when the water is ready: the wait on your bottle's own label does, or CDC's wait of at least 30 minutes when the label gives no drinking-water directions.

safety_notes.text: If treated water tastes too strongly of chlorine, pour it from one clean container to another and let it stand for a few hours before you drink it.

safety_notes.text: Do not use water with floating material, a dark color or a questionable smell, and remember that neither straining nor disinfection removes heavy metals, salts or most chemicals.
